questions.q: What field on the Marks card is unique to pie charts, and what does it control?
options: Angle — it's the pie-specific equivalent of an axis, turning a measure's value into a slice's size
Detail — it controls how many marks appear in the view
Path — it controls the order points connect in a line
Shape — it determines the icon used for each mark
questions.explain: Angle is the field that appears on the Marks card specifically for pie charts, converting a measure's value into how large a slice is drawn.

questions.q: According to Tableau's own guidance, roughly how many unique slices should a pie chart be kept to?
options: No more than about five
Exactly two, no more and no fewer
There is no practical limit
At least twenty for statistical validity
questions.explain: Tableau's own documentation recommends keeping pie charts to a small number of slices, ideally five or fewer, since more than that makes slices too close in size to compare by eye.

questions.q: What is the treemap's real advantage over a pie chart, per this lesson?
options: It can encode two measures at once — one via rectangle size, another via color — where a pie chart effectively encodes only one via angle
Treemaps require no dimension at all
Treemaps automatically sort by alphabetical order only
Treemaps can only be built from geographic data
questions.explain: A treemap keeps one measure driving rectangle size while a second measure (like Profit) drives color — a pie chart's single Angle field can't do that.

questions.q: Does Tableau have a built-in, native donut chart type?
options: No — there's no icon for it in Show Me and no dedicated official Tableau help page for it; it's a community workaround, not a shipped feature
Yes, it's the third icon in the Show Me panel
Yes, but only in Tableau Public, not Tableau Desktop
Yes, it was added as the default replacement for pie charts
questions.explain: Tableau ships no native donut chart type — building one requires manually layering two pie marks on a dual, synchronized axis, a widely-used but unofficial workaround.

questions.q: What is the standard technique for building a donut chart described in this lesson?
options: Layer a second pie mark on the same measure axis, strip its color and shrink its size, then set the axis to dual and synchronized so the smaller circle masks the center of the larger pie
Change the mark type directly to 'Donut' on the Marks card
Apply a circular blur filter to an existing pie chart image
Use the Format menu's 'Punch Hole' option on any pie chart
questions.explain: The workaround layers a second, smaller, solid-colored pie on a synchronized dual axis so it sits centered on top of the first pie, visually punching a hole through its middle.
